web_evidence.title: The French Lieutenant's Woman — Vintage Classics sample
web_evidence.note: The authorized 51-page publisher sample contains sustained chapters externally narrating Charles, Ernestina, Sarah, and Mrs Poulteney as he/she/they. Occasional 'I write' commentary belongs to the same intrusive authorial voice and does not make the Victorian action homodiegetic.

web_evidence.title: Authorial Intrusion as a Technique of Self-Conscious Narration in the English Novel
web_evidence.note: This Boğaziçi University dissertation explicitly identifies the book's narrator as omniscient, intrusive, and third-person. It treats the narrator's later corporeal appearances as metafictional episodes within that authorial technique.

web_evidence.title: Author-Narrator in John Fowles' The French Lieutenant's Woman
web_evidence.note: The scholarly article describes a traditional omniscient author-narrator, explains that textual 'I' usually marks authorial interludes, and separately discusses the author's late appearance as a minor metafictional character.

web_evidence.title: Narration and Focalization: The Quiet American, A Severed Head, and The French Lieutenant's Woman
web_evidence.note: The analysis explicitly calls the book third-person omniscient and documents its movement among the focalizations of Charles, Mrs Poulteney, and Ernestina.

web_evidence.title: Neo-Victorian Studies
web_evidence.note: This Cambridge review essay calls Fowles's voice a first-person narrator, reflecting the alternative convention of classifying an overt narrator by self-reference rather than by participation in the narrated action.

web_evidence.title: The French Lieutenant's Woman Literary Elements
web_evidence.note: This study guide calls the novel first-person despite its omniscient-third appearance and treats the narrator's late physical manifestations as minor-character appearances; this is contrary terminology relevant to the edge case.

Follow-up research found a real terminology split: some sources classify the overt authorial 'I' grammatically as first person, while structural sources classify the controlling story narration as omniscient third person.
person_note: The controlling Victorian story is sustained external narration of Charles, Sarah, Ernestina, and other characters, with mobile omniscient focalization. The narrator's conspicuous 'I' supplies authorial, historical, and metafictional commentary; it does not retrospectively tell a plot in which that narrator is a sustained participant. The late bearded-man appearance and clock manipulation are brief metaleptic embodiments of the novelist, not an autonomous first-person story strand, so they do not make the book FIRST or ALTERNATING under the base-narration criterion. The quotes and authorized opening therefore support THIRD. Confidence is medium because credible criticism uses competing terminology and sometimes calls the overt author-narrator first person or a minor character, although the underlying narrative structure is consistently described.
